newsitem.title: UK: British Conservatives in post-election bloodletting.
newsitem.headline: British Conservatives in post-election bloodletting.

text.p: A former Conservative minister launched a vitriolic attack on her former boss on Monday, rubbing salt in the wounds of a party still in shock after its humiliating defeat in Britain's May 1 election.

Former prisons minister Ann Widdecombe ripped into Michael Howard, ex-Home Secretary (interior minister) and one of six contenders for the Conservative leadership, accusing him of misleading parliament after sacking the head of the prisons service in 1995.
Howard looked ashen-faced and other Conservative MPs sat glumly as Widdecombe made good on her promise to do what she could to wreck her former boss's leadership hopes.

"I'm aware that I probably won't be forgiven for this by some people on this side of the House until the day I leave parliament. But I'm also aware that if I hadn't done what I've done today then I wouldn't have forgiven myself until I left Parliament and beyond," she said.

The dramatic 45-minute speech, dripping with contempt, recalled the onslaught in 1993 on John Major by his sacked finance minister Norman Lamont, who made the ex-prime minister squirm by telling him he was in office but no longer in power.

The crux of Widdecombe's case is that Howard had in effect overruled the former head of the prisons service, Derek Lewis, and ordered the suspension of the governor of Parkhurst prison in southern England after a serious escape.
In a debate in parliament in October 1995, Howard denied telling Lewis to suspend the Parkhurst governor, but Widdecombe said there was strong documentary evidence to the contrary.

Howard said he would respond to Widdecombe's charges in the House of Commons later on Monday, but several Conservatives said her attack had probably doomed the ex-home secretary's chances of succeeding Major, who announced he was quitting on May 2.

In addition to the six declared contenders, Tom King, 63, a former defence and Northern Ireland secretary, said he would consider standing as a caretaker candidate if the party decided to delay the leadership election, due to take place next month.
Faced with a party at war with itself, King told the Western Daily Press: "It is obviously a tough assignment for anybody.

"If enough people asked me to do it, I would think about it seriously." King, who served as a minister from 1979 to 1992, said he backed the idea of an interim leader to give the party time to involve all members in selecting the leader.
Currently, the leader is elected by Conservative MPs. Local associations are consulted but have no vote.
But Labour's landslide victory left the Conservatives -- once renowned as the most successful election-winning machine in the world -- with only 164 surviving MPs.

Other leadership candidates have seized on this. They want the party to learn lessons from new Prime Minister Tony Blair, who ruthlessly overhauled Labour by updating its policies and introducing more party democracy on its road to power.
The leaders in the race are former finance minister Kenneth Clarke and youthful former Welsh secretary William Hague.
